newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS - China stock markets plunge on fresh crackdown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - China stock markets plunge on fresh crackdown.

text.p: Beijing finally brought China's recalcitrant stock markets to heel on Friday, pushing prices down with the announcement of a huge new listing quota and the suspension of trading in the shares of several firms.
Shenzhen's domestic A share index plunged 9.33 percent to end at 467.37 and Shanghai's A shares were down 7.24 percent to 1,375.910.
Foreign exchange B shares were dragged down too, falling 7.8 percent to 159.07 in Shenzhen and 4.88 percent to 84.438 in Shanghai.
"The empire strikes back," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
"The two measures showed the government's strong determination to curb the stock markets, which resulted in panic selling," said a local broker.
The markets fell sharply at the opening on news that the government had approved a 30 billion yuan quota of new share issues for 1997, double the 1996 quota, but recovered most of the losses by noon.

Then authorities struck with the second measure -- the suspension of trading in the A shares of two firms on the Shanghai exchange and two in Shenzhen to allow for investigation into sharp fluctuations in share prices in recent days.
"People are dumping shares which have risen sharply in the past few days after the stock exchange suspended the two heavy gainers," an analyst at China Guotai Securities in Shenzhen said.
"This was the last straw for the markets today," said an A share trader. "Rumours immediately began to swirl around saying more measures to cool down the markets will follow."

Beijing has become increasingly impatient with the stock markets in recent weeks following months of strong rises, despite continual warnings from the authorities about over-heating and the risks of stock investments.
But analysts said that sentiment on the markets remained fundamentally positive, with the economic outlook good, inflation low and China due to regain sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1.
Many analysts and investors also took the view that the government's decision to expand the market through a new wave of share issues was a positive factor.
The clean-up of irregularities also helps to speed the maturation of China's young stock exchanges, analysts said.
"However painful this is in the short-term, it's good for the Chinese share markets long-term," said a stock analyst in Shanghai.

The chief economist of the State Statistical Bureau in Beijing, Qiu Xiaohua, told reporters that the government had been forced to take measures because of the high risks inherent in the volatility of the equity markets.

"Big rises and big falls are detrimental to social stability," Qiu said. "It's not that the government is very worried about the problem. Rather, the government wants to make the stock markets develop in a stable and healthy manner and do not become distorted."
